title: The phone that became a bank

thumb.headline: How a text message pulled 194,000 homes out of poverty

beats.narration: In 2007, a Kenyan phone network launched a simple way to send money by text message.
No bank branch. No account book. Just a basic phone and a corner shop agent.
Researchers followed sixteen hundred households for years, and what they found surprised even them.

visual.label: Kenyan households lifted out of extreme poverty

beats.narration: This is the story of M-Pesa, and of the women who used it to rewrite their futures.

visual.title: The phone that became a bank

beats.narration: Before mobile money, sending cash across Kenya meant a long bus ride, a trusted friend, or a costly transfer office.
For millions of rural families, the nearest bank was simply too far away, and too expensive to use.
M-Pesa changed the route. Cash went in at a local agent, travelled as a text message, and came out at another agent hundreds of kilometres away.
Today the service counts more than twenty five million users, supported by over one hundred and twenty thousand agents.
Economists Tavneet Suri of MIT and William Jack of Georgetown wanted to know whether this convenience changed lives, or only habits.

visual.headline: Mobile money and the poverty line
visual.deck: A long-run study of 1,600 Kenyan households

beats.narration: They compared communities that gained agents quickly with communities that waited longer, tracking the same families from 2008 onward.

visual.heading: How the study worked
bullets: About 1,600 households surveyed over several years
Areas with more agents compared to areas with fewer
Extreme poverty measured at $1.25 a day

beats.narration: The result: about two percent of Kenyan households, roughly one hundred and ninety four thousand, moved out of extreme poverty.

visual.label: of all Kenyan households left extreme poverty

beats.narration: Saving became easier too. Households with more agents nearby saw savings rise by around twenty two percent.

segments.title: The women who led the change

beats.narration: The strongest effects appeared in households headed by women.
Where agent numbers grew, daily spending per person in these homes rose about eighteen and a half percent, and extreme poverty among them fell by more than nine percent.
Around one hundred and eighty five thousand women left farming for business and retail work.
A safe place to keep money meant fewer risks, more choices, and the freedom to build something of their own.
Kenya's experiment did not stay in Kenya.
By 2015, more than two hundred and seventy mobile money services were running in ninety three countries, with an estimated four hundred and eleven million accounts.
The lesson is simple. When technology meets people where they already are, it can open doors that institutions never reached.

outro.narration: Technology changes lives when it reaches the people who need it most. For more stories of tech with real impact, visit T and I News.
outro.line: Technology changes lives when it reaches the people who need it most.
